definition: A language-model evaluation metric equal to the inverse probability of a test corpus, normalized per word.
details: Lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to held-out text, i.e. it “surprises” less. It is the exponential of average negative log-likelihood and is standard for comparing language models, though it correlates only loosely with quality on downstream tasks such as generation or reasoning.

explainer.lead: Perplexity is a language-model evaluation metric equal to the inverse probability of a test corpus, normalized per word. Lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to held-out text and is less surprised by it.

tiers.eli5: It measures how surprised a language model is by text it has not seen; the less surprised it is, the better the score.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it as a standard way to compare language models on held-out text, computed as the exponential of average negative log-likelihood. The pitfall is that it correlates only loosely with quality on downstream tasks such as generation or reasoning.
tiers.paperLevel: Perplexity is the inverse probability of a test corpus normalized per word; it equals the exponential of average negative log-likelihood. Known limit: loose correlation with downstream generation and reasoning quality.

explainer.example: A model that assigns higher probability to a held-out corpus than another model gets the lower perplexity and is judged less surprised by that text.
